title: 'Angh' Wins TIFF Platform Award, Earns Path to 2027 Oscars Race
excerpt: Theja Rio's debut feature — the only Indian film in TIFF's auteur-driven Platform competition — becomes eligible for the Oscars' International Feature race under new Academy rules.
body:
• Theja Rio's "Angh" won the Platform Prize at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival — the top honor in the festival's auteur-driven competitive section, and the only Indian film selected for it this year.
  • Under new Academy rules, the Platform win gives the Nagaland-set drama a direct qualifying route into the International Feature Film race at the 99th Oscars in 2027, independent of India's official submission.
  • The win carries the CAD $20,000 Platform prize, awarded by a five-member jury led by Pablo Trapero that praised the film's "strength of filmmaking" and "deeply resonant portrait of a world."
https://youtube.com/watch?v=iDmOgiyxO8M

"Angh," the feature directorial debut of Nagaland filmmaker Theja Rio, has won the Platform Prize at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival — and with it, a direct path into contention for the International Feature Film Oscar at the 99th Academy Awards. The film was the only Indian title selected for this year's Platform competition, the festival's auteur-driven section honoring bold directorial visions and distinctive cinematic storytelling.

The win was announced over the weekend as TIFF 2026 closed. In addition to the prestige, the Platform Prize comes with a CAD $20,000 award and — for the first time, under this year's expanded program — automatic entry into the Oscars' international feature race for 2027, according to Variety.

Context & Background

Launched in 2015 and inspired by Jia Zhang-ke's groundbreaking film of the same name, the Platform Prize honors filmmakers with strong directorial vision. This year's 12-title program expanded alongside the section's new Oscar-qualifying status. The five-member international jury was led by president Pablo Trapero, alongside Amma Asante, Sylvia Chang, Luc Déry, and Albert Lee. The jury singled out "Angh" for its refreshing perspective, strength of filmmaking, and deeply resonant portrait of a world — along with the filmmaker's vision, audacity, and courage. A Special Jury Award went to Amanda Kernell's "Brace Your Heart" ("Garrat Du Váimmu").

For Rio, 31, the win is the culmination of a long road with this story. Born Thejavituo Rio in Kohima, Nagaland, and trained at the National Film and Television School, he made a short-film version of "Angh" in 2021 that earned a special mention in the international competition at the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival. The feature premiered at TIFF to an overwhelming response from the jury, media, and audiences, with international and domestic sales rights acquired by Jungle Book Studio ahead of the premiere.

The Film

Set against the backdrop of 1960s Nagaland, "Angh" follows an ageing Konyak village chief and his son, among the last people holding on to their ancestral faith and way of life as their world undergoes profound change. Shot on 16mm film, it features an Indigenous Naga cast alongside BAFTA-winning actor Douglas Henshall. The film was produced by Nancy Nisa Beso and Rio, with Gaurav Dhingra as executive producer.

"I am aware that it is rare for a debut film to receive this kind of recognition, and all I can say is that we made Angh with a lot of love — for the place I come from, for my people and for our culture."

— Theja Rio, Director of "Angh"

TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey described the film as "a magnificent film" and "a really singular piece of work" — high praise from the head of a festival where the Platform section sits alongside the audience-driven People's Choice race as a marker of films to watch through awards season.

Why the Oscar Route Matters

The "automatic" part of the win is what elevates it beyond a festival trophy. Under new rules for the 99th Academy Awards, non-English-language films can reach International Feature Film consideration through two routes: selection by an Academy-approved country or regional committee, or by winning a designated award at one of six qualifying international festivals. TIFF's Platform Award is one of those qualifying prizes, alongside designated awards at Berlin, Busan, Cannes, Sundance, and Venice. That means "Angh" can now enter International Feature consideration independently of India's official submission — subject to compliance with the category's remaining requirements. The two tracks are separate: India's official entry, chosen by the Film Federation of India, remains its own decision.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora — and especially the large South Asian community that makes TIFF one of the most-attended film festivals in the world — "Angh" is a milestone of representation. Northeast Indian cinema, and Nagaland in particular, rarely reaches global stages; here is a first-time director from Kohima, telling a story rooted in Konyak culture in a film shot on 16mm with an Indigenous cast, winning a top prize in Toronto. For diaspora film communities in Toronto, New York, and the Bay Area, this is the kind of breakthrough that turns a festival win into a hometown celebration.

What's Next

"Angh" must still satisfy the Academy's remaining eligibility requirements for the International Feature category, and the industry will watch whether Jungle Book Studio mounts a full awards-season campaign. Domestically, the question is distribution: a theatrical release in India, where a Nagaland-set art-house film faces a very different market than the festival circuit, will test whether the TIFF glow translates into audiences at home. Either way, Rio has already made history — a debut feature from Nagaland with a direct line to the Oscars is a sentence Indian cinema has never written before.
